opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, because I'm very sympathetic to the worry that "long-term speculative bet" can become a catch-all excuse for working on whatever you find intellectually exciting. So I try to hold AI to a pretty demanding standard.

The way I'd frame it is that most long-term causes ask you to believe something like: "There's some event far in the future, and if we act now, we can nudge how it goes." The problem is usually that the causal chain is really long and murky. You're trying to affect something decades or centuries away through many steps you can't observe.

What makes AI feel different to me, and this is a big part of why I've shifted so much of my attention toward it, is that I don't actually think it's that far away. When I look at the trajectory of the technology, the amount of investment, and rough attempts to estimate when we might get systems that can do most of what humans do to advance science and technology, I end up thinking there's a real chance this happens within the next couple of decades. Plausibly sooner. That changes the calculus a lot. You're not trying to influence the year 2300. You're trying to influence a transition that might happen while most of us are still working.

And if it does happen, I think it could be one of the most consequential events in history. You could get explosive acceleration in scientific and economic progress. That could be wonderful, but it could also mean that whatever values, power structures, or mistakes are locked in during that transition get amplified enormously. There's also the concern of AI systems themselves having goals that aren't what we intended, which I take seriously. When you combine "potentially very soon" with "potentially extraordinarily high stakes," it just stands out from other speculative bets.

Now, I want to be honest about the weaknesses. A lot of this rests on forecasts that are genuinely uncertain, and reasonable people disagree. It's also hard to know what actually helps. Some well-intentioned work could even make things worse, for example by accelerating capabilities or creating a race dynamic. So I don't think the case for AI is "this is obviously the right bet." It's more that, compared to other long-term causes, it scores unusually well on both proximity and stakes, and the field is still small enough that thoughtful people can make a real difference.

Compared to something like global health, where you have strong evidence and clear feedback loops, AI work is much more of a leap. I still think global health is a fantastic thing to work on, and I don't want people to feel they have to drop it. But if you're already open to the idea that we should take big, uncertain bets on shaping the long-run future, I'd argue AI is where that reasoning points most strongly right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the comparison points most strongly toward AI and explains that the speaker has shifted much of their attention to it.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as potentially extraordinarily high stakes and says it scores unusually well on stakes compared with other long-term causes.

r003.rationale: It contrasts other causes’ long, murky causal chains with AI’s nearer transition and says the field is small enough for thoughtful people to make a real difference.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that makes AI stand out to me is that it's a speculative, long-term bet that has an unusually concrete story attached to it. A lot of the causes that fall under this "longtermist" umbrella, the pitch goes something like: "The future could be very big, very long, and very valuable, so even a tiny chance of affecting it is worth a lot." And I basically buy that argument, but it has this uncomfortable property where it can justify almost anything. You can tell yourself a story about how working on asteroid deflection or improving institutional decision-making or whatever is going to compound over thousands of years, and it's really hard to check whether you're fooling yourself.

With AI, I don't think you need the fancy philosophy to get to "this is a big deal." The claim I'd make is something like: there's a real chance, within our lifetimes, that we build systems that can do most of what humans do to advance science and technology, and if that happens, you get something that looks more like the agricultural revolution or the industrial revolution than like a normal technology rollout. And the thing about those transitions is that the people who were around for them, and the choices they made, actually mattered a lot for how things went. So I don't need to argue "one in a trillion chance times a trillion years of value." I can just say: there's a decent chance of the most important event in human history happening relatively soon, and it's not clear anyone's really prepared for it.

That said, I want to be honest about the weaknesses. It's still a forecast. I could be wrong about timelines, I could be wrong about how transformative it is, and even if I'm right about both, it's genuinely unclear which actions today help versus hurt. Compare that to something like global health, where you can run a randomized trial, see that bednets reduce child mortality, and then just fund the thing. AI work doesn't have that feedback loop, and I think people in this space should hold that discomfort rather than paper over it.

So the way I'd frame the comparison is: among the speculative, future-oriented bets, AI is the one where the case rests least on exotic reasoning and most on a fairly plausible empirical claim about where technology is heading. That's what moved me from "this seems weird and sci-fi" to "this is where I'd put a lot of my own effort." But I also think it's a mistake to treat it as the only thing worth doing. If you're the kind of person who finds you can't make progress without clear feedback on whether you're helping, that's a legitimate reason to work on something more tractable, and I'd rather have people doing excellent work on measurable problems than mediocre, demoralized work on AI because they felt they were supposed to.

r001.rationale: The speaker says AI is where they would put much of their own effort, specifically when comparing speculative, future-oriented bets.

r002.rationale: The speaker describes AI as having a decent chance of producing “the most important event in human history,” which communicates unusually high consequence relative to the other causes under discussion.

r003.rationale: The speaker calls the empirical case for AI more plausible, but says it is unclear which AI actions help or hurt. They do not judge AI work itself more likely to achieve impact than work on other speculative causes.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much of the case depends on a particular story about the distant future. You can tell a story where some action today has enormous consequences thousands of years from now, but that alone doesn’t give me much confidence that it’s the right action. You want to understand why this is a particularly good opportunity to have an influence, and why the influence is likely to be positive.

With AI, the thing that makes it stand out to me is the possibility that we’re developing a technology that could automate a lot of the work humans do to advance science and technology. If that happens, it could be an extraordinarily consequential transition. And there are people making decisions about how to develop these systems today. So there’s a connection between something happening now, something we can potentially affect, and a very large change in the world.

That doesn’t mean the case is airtight. There’s uncertainty about when this happens, what the problems will look like, and which interventions will help. I’d distinguish being convinced that AI deserves a lot of attention from being convinced that any particular AI project is a good use of resources.

But I don’t see it as just another argument that says, ‘The future is enormous, so this speculative thing must be important.’ The more compelling argument is that this particular development could be a major turning point, and we may have a relatively unusual opportunity to help it go better.

r001.rationale: The response says AI deserves attention and stands out, but does not express a preference for working on AI over the other causes.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as potentially extraordinarily consequential, but does not judge it more consequential than the other long-term speculative causes.

r003.rationale: It notes that AI decisions today may be influenceable, but does not judge AI work more likely to achieve impact than the other causes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much of a feedback loop you can get, even when the thing you ultimately care about is very far away. There’s a big difference between saying, “Here’s something that could matter enormously in a hundred years,” and saying, “Here’s a problem where we can do work today, learn something, and have a better idea of what to do next.”

AI has some advantages there. There’s an actual technology being developed, there are people building it, and there are questions you can investigate about how these systems behave and how to make them more reliable. You don’t have to get every part of the long-term story right for some of that work to be useful.

That doesn’t mean we have a good feedback loop on the ultimate question of whether we’re reducing existential risk. We don’t. And I worry about people treating a compelling story about the future as if it were strong evidence for a particular intervention.

So I wouldn’t put all speculative long-term work in one bucket. I’d look at the particular opportunity: What do you have to believe for this to help? What could you learn over the next few years? Would you notice if your approach wasn’t working? I think some work on AI looks unusually good by those standards, but that’s a case for being selective about the work, rather than just deciding that anything labelled AI safety must be a good bet.

r001.rationale: The response says some AI work looks unusually good compared with speculative long-term work, expressing a selective preference for it.

r002.rationale: It does not say AI is more consequential than the other long-term causes.

r003.rationale: It highlights opportunities to learn and assess AI work, but does not clearly judge that AI work is more likely to achieve impact than the other causes.
